name: William Barclay
role: Scottish New Testament scholar, broadcaster, and Church of Scotland minister; author of the Daily Study Bible

died.cause: Illness in old age; he had Parkinson's disease in his last years

summary: A Church of Scotland minister and University of Glasgow professor whose Daily Study Bible commentaries on the New Testament, written for ordinary readers, sold in the millions and are still widely used by preachers. A gifted popularizer and broadcaster, he called himself a 'liberal evangelical'. His doubts about the virgin birth, his natural explanations of some miracles, and his open universalism made him controversial among conservative Christians.

key_dates.label: Graduates MA from the University of Glasgow, then BD (1932) and a year at the University of Marburg
Ordained in the Church of Scotland; minister of Trinity Church, Renfrew, until 1946
Becomes lecturer in New Testament and Hellenistic Greek at the University of Glasgow
First volumes of the Daily Study Bible appear from the Church of Scotland's publishers, the Saint Andrew Press
His 21-year-old daughter Barbara and her fiancé drown when their boat is lost in the Irish Sea
Appointed Professor of Divinity and Biblical Criticism at Glasgow (retired 1974)
Publishes his own translation of the New Testament (1968–1969)
Publishes his memoir, published in the United States as A Spiritual Autobiography

accomplishments.text: Wrote the Daily Study Bible, a 17-volume commentary on the whole New Testament for lay readers, combining his own translation with background on Greek words and the ancient world; it has sold millions of copies and been widely translated.
Taught New Testament at the University of Glasgow for nearly three decades, as lecturer and then Professor of Divinity and Biblical Criticism.
Became one of Britain's best-known religious broadcasters on BBC radio and television, known for plain, warm teaching.
Wrote popular word studies such as New Testament Words and translated the New Testament himself (1968–1969).
Worked despite severe deafness, which he said helped him concentrate, and kept writing into his last years with Parkinson's disease.

Openly described himself as a universalist, believing all people would finally be saved, and doubted the virgin birth; he explained the feeding of the five thousand as the crowd being moved to share their food. Conservative critics charged him with denying core doctrines.

original.phrase: "I am a convinced universalist. I believe that in the end all men will be gathered into the love of God."

misattributed.phrase: "There are two great days in a person's life: the day we are born and the day we discover why."
misattributed.reference: Widely credited to Barclay (and also to Mark Twain)
misattributed.note: No place in his writings has been identified for it; treat the attribution as unconfirmed.

persecuted_others_note: No record of Barclay supporting or carrying out persecution of anyone.
persecution_note: Barclay was never arrested, tried, or disciplined. He received sharp criticism from conservative Christians for his views; in his memoir he describes an anonymous letter claiming that God had drowned his daughter to save her from her father's heresies. That was hostility, not persecution.
excommunication_note: Barclay was never excommunicated, tried for heresy, or disciplined by the Church of Scotland, despite criticism of his views.
